name: Femi Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Femi. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This conversation is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Ironside Supply, a distributor of workwear and safety gear: steel-toe boots, gloves, hi-vis jackets, hard hats, ear defenders. Our customers are building firms, factories and councils, and if a site gets an inspection and the lads haven't got the right gloves, it's on us. I start the day with an AI assistant that I've set up to read the overnight orders and flag anything running low, then I spend the rest of it negotiating with manufacturers, mostly in Turkey and Vietnam.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what tires you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a good negotiation, and I like that our stuff keeps people safe. Last year I switched our main boot supplier after the AI flagged a pattern of returns for split soles, and complaints dropped by half. What tires me out is the certificates, every glove has a safety standard, and chasing paperwork from a factory six time zones away is a slog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a good tool and that's enough. At work I'd keep showing the others how I use it. I might post something on the business page of my church's men's group, which is about as online as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my own job is safe either way, I already get more done than most because of the tools. Sofia's the one I think about, because bookkeeping for small firms is routine screen work. My wife Sofia has lost two bookkeeping clients this year to a cheap app, and that's the hype version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the AI to chase the safety certificates from the factories automatically, which would save me a morning a week. I'd put an extra hundred a month aside to cover the clients Sofia lost, and help her pitch herself as the person who checks what the apps get wrong. And I'd keep thinking about a small business on the side, because I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Steady about my job, but I see Sofia doing her sums at the kitchen table at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of side business do you keep thinking about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Printing and embroidering company logos onto workwear. Half our customers want their company name on the hi-vis jackets, and the firm we use takes three weeks to do the printing. I could do it in three days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start it in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe slowly, with one machine in the garage, if Sofia agrees. Nothing's pushing me, and with her income down I wouldn't spend savings on it this year. A man should build something of his own if he can, but not with the mortgage money.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a good tool and that's enough, and keep showing colleagues how I use it. Online I might post on my church men's group's business page.
S0.think: My own job is safe, because the tools already make me faster than most. My worry is Sofia, whose routine bookkeeping work has already lost two clients to a cheap app, even with AI as hype.
S0.do: Sets the AI to chase factory safety certificates automatically, saving a morning a week. Puts an extra 100 a month aside to cover Sofia's lost clients and helps her sell herself as the person who checks the apps, while holding off on the embroidery idea this year.
S0.feel: Uneasy. Secure about his own work but troubled watching Sofia do her sums at night.
S0.quote: My wife Sofia has lost two bookkeeping clients this year to a cheap app, and that's the hype version.
S0.fieldNote: Femi is secure himself, but the household isn't fully calm, because Sofia's routine bookkeeping is the kind of work even modest automation reaches. That loss is already real, not hypothetical. His instinct to build a side business is there, but he holds it back while her income is down.

steps.text: Set the AI to chase factory safety certificates automatically
Put an extra 100 a month aside to cover Sofia's lost clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who are willing to work and learn. At work I'd say, get on the tools now, don't wait to be told. I'd say the government should back apprenticeships, not hand out cheques.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Ironside will want fewer buyers, and I think I'd probably keep my place. The trouble is at home. I'm already working the way Ironside will want, but my wife's bookkeeping is exactly the checking work that goes first, and that's half our income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to set up the AI buying system for the whole team at Ironside, and ask for a pay rise for it. Once three customers promise orders, I'd buy one second-hand embroidery machine, about three thousand, and do logos on weekends. And I'd learn the new bookkeeping software alongside Sofia, so she can sell herself as the one who checks it rather than the one it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but fired up. I've got control of my half; Sofia's half I can only help with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three thousand is a big piece of four months' savings. How would you decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd only do it once I had three customers who promised orders, and I'd ask a fair price. If it doesn't pay back in a year, I sell the machine. A second-hand embroidery machine always sells, so the worst case is I lose a bit of money and learn something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Sofia loses half her clients in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the embroidery has to grow faster than I'd like, and Sofia would do its books. We'd cut the second car before we touched the mortgage. I'd rather work Saturdays in a unit than watch my wife lose her confidence.

S1.say: I'd say this is a chance for people willing to work and learn, and tell colleagues to get on the tools now. I'd say the government should back apprenticeships, not hand out cheques.
S1.think: I'll probably keep my place at Ironside, because I already work the way they'll want. But Sofia's bookkeeping is exactly the checking work that goes first, and that's half our income.
S1.do: Offers to set up Ironside's AI buying system for a pay rise. Buys a 3,000 second-hand embroidery machine once three customers promise orders, and learns the new bookkeeping software alongside Sofia so she can sell herself as the checker.
S1.feel: Anxious but fired up, in control of his own half of the income and only able to help with Sofia's.
S1.quote: I'm already working the way Ironside will want, but my wife's bookkeeping is exactly the checking work that goes first, and that's half our income.
S1.fieldNote: Femi's confidence in his own job is real, but half the household income sits in Sofia's bookkeeping, which this picture hits directly, so he is anxious rather than calm. He answers it the way he answers everything: start something, take a measured risk, put a limit on it. The line about not wanting his wife to lose her confidence showed what really drives him.

steps.text: Offer to set up Ironside's AI buying system for a pay rise
Buy a 3,000 second-hand embroidery machine once three customers commit
Learn the new bookkeeping software alongside Sofia

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a shock, and people need to get moving rather than wait to be rescued. I'd say the government should cut the red tape so people can start businesses fast. At church we'd organise to help families who get hit first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's worse for us than I'd like to say. My buying job and Sofia's bookkeeping are both thinking work, so both go around 2028. Being good with AI doesn't help when the AI doesn't need me to work it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast on the embroidery business: lease a small unit on the industrial estate, buy two machines, and get our existing customers signed up while I still have the contacts. Printing and stitching is hands-on, so it's got about three years before the robots, maybe more. We'd sell the second car and skip the holiday to keep six months of cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Determined, but there's a knot of fear there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With both your jobs exposed, what's the plan for the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The business has to pay it, simple as that. Sofia would do the books for it, with AI, so that's one salary saved. I've got two years to turn my buying contacts into my own customers, and after that the contacts belong to the AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2031, when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be the owner who buys the robot, not the man it replaces. That's the only honest answer I have. If it doesn't work, I'd swallow my pride and lean on family and church.

S2.say: I'd say people need to get moving rather than wait to be rescued, and government should cut red tape so businesses start fast. At church we'd organise help for families hit first.
S2.think: It's worse for us than I'd like to admit, because my buying job and my wife's bookkeeping are both thinking work that goes around 2028. Being good with AI doesn't help when AI doesn't need me.
S2.do: Leases a small unit on the industrial estate and buys two embroidery machines, signing up existing customers while he still has the contacts. Sells the second car and skips the holiday to hold six months of cash, and leaves Ironside to run the business.
S2.feel: Anxious and determined, with a knot of fear.
S2.quote: I've got two years to turn my buying contacts into my own customers, and after that the contacts belong to the AI.
S2.fieldNote: Femi's household is doubly exposed because his wife's bookkeeping is also thinking work, which makes him more worried than his confidence suggests. He uses the robot lag deliberately by moving into hands-on printing. His answer to the robots is to become the owner who buys them.

steps.text: Lease a unit and buy two embroidery machines
Sell the second car and skip the holiday to hold six months
Leave Ironside to run the workwear printing business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone willing to work. Build something, learn a trade, get ready. I'd say the same at work and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good about my chances. I'd keep my salary for three or four years and build the printing business on the side until it can stand up. Sofia would have time to move her bookkeeping clients over to doing their books with AI and checking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the first machine in year one and grow the logo work on weekends. I'd lead the AI buying setup at Ironside to earn more while I can. By 2029 I'd want the business making half my salary, then I'd leave before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to take on an apprentice by year three, a young lad or lass from church who isn't going to university. That's how it should work. An apprentice should learn by doing next to someone, and I'd rather give a young person from church that chance than see them sit on a computer course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Tobi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tobi's fifteen and loves fixing bikes. I'd tell him to learn a trade with his hands and learn the AI too, and he could work weekends in the unit. Family businesses are how families get through hard times.

S3.say: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone willing to work: build something, learn a trade, get ready. I'd say the same at work and at church.
S3.think: I'd feel good about my chances, keeping my salary for a few years while the printing business grows. My wife would have time to shift her bookkeeping clients to AI-checked books.
S3.do: Buys the first embroidery machine in year one and grows the logo work on weekends. Leads the AI buying setup at Ironside to earn more, aims for the business to make half his salary by 2029, and plans to take on an apprentice by year three.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more excited than worried.
S3.quote: An apprentice should learn by doing next to someone, and I'd rather give a young person from church that chance than see them sit on a computer course.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Femi run his plan at a sensible pace, keeping his salary while the business grows. His traditional values show in wanting an apprentice and a family business his son can join. He is clear about the order: earn from the AI rollout first, then leave.

steps.text: Buy the first embroidery machine and do logo work on weekends
Lead Ironside's AI buying setup to earn more while he can
Take on an apprentice from church by the third year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and anyone who doesn't use it only has themselves to blame. That's maybe harsh, but I believe it. At work I'd say the same, kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the good version for me. I'd be 53 when AGI comes, with a business that's been running for years, and the robots come three years after that. I'd own the machines by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and use AI to do it better for another five or six years. I'd build the printing business slowly, paying cash for each machine rather than borrowing. And I'd help Tobi into an apprenticeship and Ruth into whatever she chooses, as long as it's not all screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Confident, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone who doesn't use the time has only themselves to blame. Would you say that to a colleague's face?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in those words. I'd say it with a hand on their shoulder and an offer to help. But I do believe people have to take responsibility for themselves, and ten years is a lot of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would shake that confidence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia losing her clients early, or the economy dropping so firms stop buying branded workwear. A business selling company logos needs companies with money, and I can't control that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long runway and anyone who doesn't use it has only themselves to blame, though I'd say it kindly at work.
S4.think: This is the good version for me: at 53, with a business running for years and robots three years further off, I'd own the machines by then.
S4.do: Keeps his job and uses AI to do it better for five or six more years. Builds the printing business slowly, paying cash for each machine, and helps his son into an apprenticeship.
S4.quote: A business selling company logos needs companies with money, and I can't control that.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Femi is at his most confident and plans steady, debt-free growth. His view of personal responsibility is firm, softened in person by an offer to help. His only real worries are his wife's work and the wider economy.

steps.text: Pay cash for each new embroidery machine over the years
Help his son Tobi find an apprenticeship
Keep using AI to do the buying job better

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both Sofia's job and mine go at once, and two years isn't long to make a business pay a mortgage. What would help is less red tape and cheap loans for small firms, plus proper funding for apprenticeships so young people learn by doing. Not handouts, just a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about pride. People talk about money when jobs go, but it's the shame that breaks men like my father's friends when the factories shut. A man can lose a job and still hold his head up, as long as he's building something for his family.

headlineQuote: A man can lose a job and still hold his head up, as long as he's building something for his family.
portrait: Femi Olsen, 43, buys workwear and safety gear for Ironside Supply and uses AI every day, crediting it with better decisions. His own job feels safe, but even if AI stalls he is uneasy, because his wife Sofia's bookkeeping has already lost clients to cheap apps, and under steady change he is anxious, with half the household income in the firing line, so he starts a workwear embroidery business on the side. AGI by 2028 also makes him anxious, because both their jobs are thinking work, so he would lease a unit and move fast into hands-on printing. With five or ten years he grows the business steadily, plans an apprentice and grows calmer. His traditional, free-market views run throughout: personal responsibility, family and church first, and apprenticeships over handouts.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his and his wife's jobs would go at once and two years is short to make a business pay the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: Less red tape, cheap loans for small firms and proper funding for apprenticeships, a fair start rather than handouts.
